item.passage:
The frost had been busy again. Every April, after the field behind the barn was plowed, it came up looking as if someone had scattered potatoes across it overnight, except that the potatoes were stones. Uncle Abel drove the tractor at a walking pace, towing the stoneboat, a flat sled of planks on iron runners, and Jonah walked beside it, lifting rocks and dropping them onto the boards.

"We picked this whole field last spring," Jonah said around noon. He had said it twice already that morning. "Every stone."

Uncle Abel kept his eyes on the furrow. "Frost pushes them up. Water gets under a stone in the fall and freezes, and the ice lifts it a little. Then dirt slides in underneath before it can settle back. Do that fifty winters and you get a crop."

By two o'clock Jonah had worked out a system. The big stones, the ones the size of a loaf of bread or a bucket, he rolled onto the boards with both arms. The small ones, about the size of an egg, he stepped over. There were hundreds of those, and each one cost a bend at the waist for almost nothing. Working that way, he reached the far fence an hour before the light began to go, and he stood there with his gloves off, waiting for his uncle to say something about the time.

Uncle Abel shut off the engine. He climbed down, walked twenty steps back along the row, and bent over. When he straightened up, he was holding a stone about the size of an egg. He carried it to the fence, where the old mower sat in the weeds, and set it on the cutter bar beside three blades that were brighter than the rest.

"Last July," he said, "one of these went through the mower in the far corner. Snapped three sections. I spent the afternoon riveting new ones on, and the hay I'd already cut lay out in the rain that night." He picked the stone up again. "A rock the size of a bucket I can see from the seat and steer around. These hide in the grass."

Jonah looked back down the field. In the low light the egg-sized stones threw small shadows, and now that he was looking for them, they were everywhere.

He put his gloves back on. They went back down the rows together with the engine off, each of them carrying a bucket, and by the time the handles were cutting into their fingers the sun was behind the woodlot. Jonah emptied his load onto the pile by the gate, a heap that had been growing there, his uncle said, since before the barn was built. The stones at the bottom were green with moss. His were the color of the field.

"Same ones next year?" Jonah asked.

"Their cousins," said Uncle Abel.

so narrow by sixty years of whetting
that it looks like the moon three nights from dark.

The summer I was thirteen, I spent six weeks shooting arrows into a bale of straw from about three steps away. The bale had a plain face, just the yellow ends of the straw packed tight and tied with twine, without rings or a gold circle to aim at. That was Mr. Ostrander's rule for every new archer at the county range: you shot at a blank bale until he said otherwise.

The other beginners quit by the second week. I stayed partly because my mother had already paid for the summer and partly because I wanted, badly, to be told I was good. Mr. Ostrander did not tell anyone that. He stood behind me with his arms crossed and said the same few words in different orders: elbow, anchor, breathe, again. When I drew the string to my chin he would lower my elbow half an inch, or tap the back of my bow hand, which meant I was gripping the bow when I should have let it rest in my palm. Then he walked off to stand behind someone else.

Every Friday I asked whether I could shoot at a real target. Every Friday he looked at the bale for a while, as if it might have an opinion, and said, "Monday, maybe."

In the fifth week I brought a paper plate from home and, while he was out in the parking lot, pinned it to a bale at twenty yards. My first arrow clipped the edge of the plate. My second sailed past the bale and skidded into the grass, and I was still hunting for it when he walked back across the lot. He took the plate down, folded it once, and put it in his jacket pocket. He said nothing about it, then or ever.

He gave me a target face at the end of the sixth week. I shot six arrows at it from twenty yards, and all six landed low and to the left, in a cluster I could have covered with my hand. I thought it was a disaster. Mr. Ostrander walked down to the target, studied it for a long moment, and came back smiling, which I had never seen him do.

"That," he said, "is the first good thing you've shot." He turned a small knob on my bow sight, a few clicks down and a few to the left. "A group I can move. A scatter I can't do anything with."

The next six arrows went into the gold or close around it. I remember that the gold felt less important than I had expected, because standing there I finally understood what the weeks at the bale had been for. The sight could only move my arrows if they all went to the same place, and until they did, there had been nothing for it to correct.

I shot for Mr. Ostrander for four more summers and heard him call something good perhaps a dozen times. I still think he could have explained the bale on the first day and saved me a paper plate and a good deal of sulking. But when I start something new now, a language or a piece of music, I find myself looking first for the bale: the stage where it does not matter where anything lands, only that it lands the same way twice.

In the autumn of 1871 the day school in Haddon Weir, a brick building of two rooms on Ash Street, taught about ninety children between the ages of six and thirteen. It taught almost none of their older brothers and sisters. By fourteen most young people in the town had gone to work in the woolen mill by the river, where a shift ran from six in the morning until six at night.

That October the younger of the two teachers, Abigail Sorrell, asked the school committee for the use of her classroom on three evenings a week. She proposed to teach reading, writing and arithmetic, free of charge, to any mill hand over fourteen who cared to come. The committee agreed on one condition: the town would not pay for lamp oil. Every evening student would have to bring oil, or the few cents it cost.

The condition sounds harsh, and it has usually been told that way. The committee's minute book suggests a plainer reason. The school money for that year had already gone on a new roof, and the spring town meeting had turned down the committee's request for more. Its members appear to have wanted the evening classes and to have had nothing to pay for them with.

Sorrell's register survives. It records twenty-three students on the first night and forty-one by December. Most were between fifteen and twenty; the oldest, a carder named Tobias Venn, gave his age as thirty-four. Each name is followed by a row of small marks, one for each evening's oil, and the marks show that the students kept the system going themselves. When a student could not pay, a neighbor on the bench often paid for two. One entry reads simply "Venn for Ada M."

Attendance followed the seasons. It was highest in January, when the mill sometimes closed for a week because ice stopped the wheel, and it fell sharply each May, when daylight lasted well past the end of a shift and many students spent those hours in their gardens. By 1874 Sorrell held classes only from October to April.

The results are harder to measure than the numbers. Sorrell noted that by the end of the first winter nineteen students could read a newspaper column aloud, and the mill's pay book shows that several former students later signed for their wages with a name where they had once made a mark. These are small figures, and the first of them comes from the teacher, who had reason to record success. Still, they are what survives, and they point the same way.

In 1879 the town built a larger school, and the committee, with money to spend at last, voted to pay for the evening lamp oil itself. Attendance at the evening classes fell by half within a year, and they closed in 1881. The register gives no reason, and it would be easy to invent one. What can be said is that for eight winters the classes had been paid for, a cup of oil at a time, by the students who sat in them.

Stay in a bath long enough and the skin on your fingertips puckers into ridges, as though the fingers had aged decades in a quarter of an hour. The change usually begins within several minutes in warm water and is clearest after something like half an hour. It shows up on the fingers, the palms, the toes and the soles of the feet, and almost nowhere else on the body.

For a long time the explanation seemed obvious. The outermost layer of skin is made mostly of dead cells packed with a protein called keratin, which soaks up water. On the fingertips that layer is especially thick, so the idea was that it swelled as it absorbed water and, because it is anchored to the tissue beneath, buckled into folds.

A clue against that idea had been in the medical record since the 1930s. Doctors noticed that when the nerve serving a finger had been cut, through injury or surgery, that finger stayed smooth in water while its neighbors wrinkled. If wrinkling were simply skin soaking up water, a cut nerve should have made no difference. Later, doctors began using a soak as a simple bedside test: a finger that stayed smooth pointed to nerve damage.

The explanation most researchers now favor gives the nervous system the central role. When the hands are soaked, nerves signal the tiny blood vessels beneath the fingertip skin to narrow. With less blood in it, the soft pad of the fingertip loses a little volume, and the skin on top, which keeps its size, is drawn down into ridges, rather as the skin of a grape folds as the fruit dries into a raisin.

If the body produces wrinkles on purpose, the wrinkles may do something useful. One proposal is that they work like the tread on a tire, channeling water away so that wet fingers grip better. In a 2013 experiment, volunteers moved small wet objects, such as marbles, from one container to another faster when their fingers were wrinkled than when they were smooth; with dry objects, wrinkling made little difference. A study published the following year, using a similar task, found no advantage at all.

So the question is open. That the wrinkles are controlled by nerves, and are more than a matter of soaking, is well supported. Why the body produces them is less settled. The grip idea is appealing, and it may yet hold up, but one successful experiment and one failed attempt to repeat it do not make a finding.
